title: Trophic rewilding influences plant–pollinator interactions through multiple pathways
content:
Synthesis and applications: Our study showed that trophic rewilding can promote diverse and abundant floral resources. This effect, in turn, increases grasslands' capacity to support diverse, active insect pollinator communities and more complex, generalized plant-pollinator interaction networks, indicating resilient and functionally robust pollination systems. Yet, our study also illustrates that herbivore-induced reductions in herbaceous vegetation height can negatively affect pollinators at local scales (14 m2). We suggest managers restore the ecological functions of large herbivores where absent and allow spatial variability in their impacts to benefit pollinators and their plant interactions.


Abstract

Large wild mammalian herbivores have a unique and profound impact on ecosystems globally but have declined widely and disproportionately throughout (pre)history. Restoring large herbivores' ecological functions is thought to promote vegetation heterogeneity, with likely cascading effects on other taxonomic groups and ecological processes. Despite increasing knowledge of large-herbivore biodiversity impacts, the direct and indirect effects of large herbivores on insect pollinators and their interactions with flowering plants remain poorly investigated. During the 2024 growing season, we used an experimental block setup at a Danish trophic rewilding site to explore how semi-wild cattle and horses indirectly—through their effects on plants and microclimate—influenced insect pollinator (morpho)species richness and activity, as well as the richness and generalization of plant–pollinator interactions compared to large-herbivore exclosures and annual mowing. Large herbivores promoted floral species richness, which, in turn, was positively related to pollinator (morpho)species richness and possibly visitation rates. Likewise, pollinator (morpho)species richness and visitation rate were positively associated with herbivore-induced increases in floral resources (nectar-sugar quantity), although only compared with exclosures. Large herbivores, however, had an equally negative indirect effect on pollinator (morpho)species richness and visitation rate by reducing the mean height of herbaceous vegetation. Finally, by promoting floral species richness, large herbivores likely increased interaction richness and network-level generalization, and thus the functional redundancy of plant–pollinator interactions. Synthesis and applications: Our study showed that trophic rewilding can promote diverse and abundant floral resources. This effect, in turn, increases grasslands' capacity to support diverse, active insect pollinator communities and more complex, generalized plant–pollinator interaction networks, indicating resilient and functionally robust pollination systems. Yet, our study also illustrates that herbivore-induced reductions in herbaceous vegetation height can negatively affect pollinators at local scales (14 m2). We suggest managers restore the ecological functions of large herbivores where absent and allow spatial variability in their impacts to benefit pollinators and their plant interactions.
